claims.text: The transport specification published as RFC 793 in September 1981, edited by Postel, states that very few assumptions are made about the reliability of the layers below it: it assumes only a simple, potentially unreliable datagram service, and should in principle operate above a wide spectrum of communication systems ranging from hard-wired connections to packet-switched or circuit-switched networks.

source.title: RFC 793, Transmission Control Protocol, J. Postel ed., September 1981; obsoleted by RFC 9293 in 2022

claims.text: That document was the ninth edition of the specification and has itself been obsoleted, replaced by RFC 9293 in 2022 — so the number most engineers cite for this protocol has not been the current specification for several years.

source.title: RFC 793, Transmission Control Protocol, J. Postel ed., September 1981; obsoleted by RFC 9293 in 2022

beats.broke: a message has to cross machines and networks that were not built together, may drop it, may reorder it, and have no common notion of who anything is
beats.fix: cut the message into independently addressed packets, give every interface a number so packets can be routed, and give every conversation on a machine a second number so arriving packets can be handed to the right program
beats.cost: the layer beneath guarantees nothing, so ordering, retransmission and duplicate detection are built above it — and every such guarantee is paid for in round trips
beats.interview: what an address identifies and what a port identifies
